How a Waffle Iron Built Nike

Recommended title: The Entire History of Nike: From a Car Trunk to a $46 Billion Feeling

9:54Est. runtime
10Parts
65Shots
1,427Words

Hook

Top hooks, yt-script score

  • 39A coach poured rubber into his wife's waffle iron. That ruined waffle iron became a 46-billion-dollar company.
  • 42Michael Jordan didn't want to sign with Nike. He wanted Adidas. Here's how Nike changed his mind and made 100 million in year one.

Look and device

Running device

A ruined waffle iron that keeps coming back as a running gag: every time Nike invents something new it sizzles, every time Nike coasts on old hits it sits cold and dusty on a shelf. A running revenue counter in the corner ticks from $8,000 to $46 billion.

Look

Upbeat business-history documentary in the house 2D style, Gumball/t-shirt character style (as in NVIDIA). Painted plates: a rainy 1960s Oregon track, a Kobe office with paper screens, a garage workshop full of shoe parts, a 1980s Chicago arena, a glassy Beaverton campus. Warm orange and teal with the swoosh as the one accent. SFX under the VO (spikes on cinder, sizzling iron, crowd roars, cash register); music only at combine.

Cold open

    In 1971, a track coach poured rubber into his wife's waffle iron. It glued shut and never made a waffle again.

    ANIMATIONRubber pours; lid slams; smoke puff and a sad sizzle.

  2. 0.02MED8.7s

    That ruined waffle iron helped start a company that now sells around 46 billion dollars of shoes and clothes a year.

    The waffle iron on a pedestal; a counter rolls up beside it.

    ~$46 BILLION / YEAR

    ANIMATIONCounter spins up; coins rain.

  3. 0.03MED6.8s

    And here's the strange part: Nike owns almost none of the factories that make its shoes.

    A Nike box with a big question mark; factories in the background with other names on them.

    ANIMATIONQuestion mark bounces on the box.

  4. 0.04MED12.1s

    This is the story of a made-up company name, a 35-dollar logo, a basketball player who wanted to sign with someone else, and a slogan with a very dark origin.

    ANIMATIONPanels slap down one by one.

Act 1: The Coach and the Runner

1:10 · 8 shots · 170 words
  1. 1.01WIDE8.3s

    Oregon, the 1950s. Bill Bowerman coached track at the University of Oregon, and he had a thing about heavy shoes.

    A rainy cinder track; a coach in a cap with a stopwatch.

    UNIVERSITY OF OREGON · 1950s

    ANIMATIONRain; runners splash past; stopwatch clicks.

  2. 1.02MED8.7s

    His maths: shave one ounce off a shoe and, over a mile of strides, a runner lifts hundreds of pounds less.

    A chalkboard with a shoe, minus one ounce, equals a pile of weights crossed out.

    -1 OUNCE = -HUNDREDS OF POUNDS

    ANIMATIONChalk scratches out the sum.

  3. 1.03MED10.9s

    So he pulled his runners' shoes apart in his workshop and rebuilt them by hand. His athletes were his test subjects, whether they liked it or not.

    A cluttered workshop, shoe parts everywhere; a runner hopping in a lopsided shoe.

    ANIMATIONHammer taps; the runner winces.

  4. 1.04MED7.2s

    One of those runners was a middle-distance man called Phil Knight. Good, not great. But he listened.

    A young runner with a notebook, nodding at the coach.

    PHIL KNIGHT

    ANIMATIONKnight scribbles; the coach gestures.

  5. 1.05MED11.3s

    At Stanford business school in 1962, Knight wrote a paper: Japanese running shoes could do to German brands like Adidas what Japanese cameras had done to German cameras.

    A paper with two columns: CAMERAS and SHOES; arrows from Japan beating Germany.

    STANFORD · 1962

    ANIMATIONPen underlines the thesis.

  6. 1.06WIDE9.8s

    That same year, aged 24, he flew to Japan and walked into the offices of Onitsuka in Kobe, makers of the Tiger running shoe.

    A plane over the Pacific, then an office with sliding screens and executives in suits.

    KOBE · 1962

    ANIMATIONDoor slides open; bows.

  7. 1.07CU8.7s

    They asked which company he represented. He didn't have one. So he made one up on the spot: Blue Ribbon Sports.

    Close on Knight sweating; a thought bubble with a blue ribbon.

    'BLUE RIBBON SPORTS'

    ANIMATIONA bead of sweat; the ribbon pops into the bubble.

  8. 1.08MED5.3s

    It worked. Onitsuka let him sell Tigers in the western United States.

    A handshake across a desk; a box of Tiger shoes slides over.

    ANIMATIONHandshake; box thump.

Act 2: Shoes From a Car Trunk

0:56 · 7 shots · 133 words
  1. 2.01MED6.4s

    In 1964, Knight and Bowerman put in 500 dollars each. Blue Ribbon Sports was real.

    Two hands each slap 500 dollars on a table.

    $500 + $500

    ANIMATIONBills slap down.

  2. 2.02WIDE7.2s

    Knight sold the shoes from the trunk of his car at track meets across the Pacific Northwest.

    A car with its trunk open at a track meet; runners queuing.

    ANIMATIONTrunk pops; boxes handed out.

  3. 2.03CU6.8s

    First year: about 1,300 pairs, roughly 8,000 dollars. He kept his day job as an accountant.

    Revenue counter in the corner shows $8,000; Knight at a ledger.

    $8,000

    ANIMATIONCounter ticks; adding-machine chatter.

  4. 2.04MED10.9s

    His first full-time employee, Jeff Johnson, wrote personal letters to customers, noted their race times and even their birthdays, and opened the first store in Santa Monica.

    A desk buried in handwritten letters; a small shopfront sign.

    JEFF JOHNSON

    ANIMATIONLetters stack up; shop bell rings.

  5. 2.05MED10.6s

    Meanwhile Bowerman wrote a little book called Jogging, which helped set off the American running boom. The coach wasn't just making shoes. He was making customers.

    A small book; behind it a park fills with joggers.

    'JOGGING'

    ANIMATIONJoggers multiply across the park.

  6. 2.06CU9.4s

    Then, in 1971, came the waffle iron. Ruined, as we saw. But its grid of squares became the waffle sole: grip without weight.

    The sealed waffle iron; peel away to reveal a sole with a waffle grid.

    THE WAFFLE SOLE

    ANIMATIONSizzle; the sole peels away cleanly.

  7. 2.07MED4.2s

    The Bowermans had to buy a new waffle iron.

    A shop receipt: 1 WAFFLE IRON.

    ANIMATIONReceipt prints out with a ding.

Act 3: A Name, a Logo, a Split

1:19 · 9 shots · 192 words
  1. 3.01MED9.1s

    By the early 1970s, Blue Ribbon and Onitsuka didn't trust each other. Each suspected the other was about to cut it out.

    Two businessmen back to back, each with a contract behind their back.

    ANIMATIONSide-eye from both; a clock ticks.

  2. 3.02MED10.6s

    Knight needed his own brand, fast. For a logo, he asked Carolyn Davidson, a design student he'd met at Portland State, for something that suggested motion.

    A student at a drawing table, sketches of curves pinned up.

    CAROLYN DAVIDSON

    ANIMATIONPencil scratches; sketches pile.

  3. 3.03CU9.4s

    At two dollars an hour, it came to 35 dollars. Knight's verdict: he didn't love it, but maybe it would grow on him.

    The swoosh on paper with a $35 price tag.

    $35

    ANIMATIONPrice tag swings.

  4. 3.04MED6.4s

    The name came even closer to the deadline. Knight wanted 'Dimension Six'. Nobody else did.

    A whiteboard with DIMENSION 6 and a row of unimpressed faces.

    DIMENSION 6?

    ANIMATIONCricket chirp.

  5. 3.05MED11.7s

    Then Jeff Johnson said a word had come to him in a dream: Nike, the Greek goddess of victory. The boxes had to be printed, so Nike it was.

    Johnson asleep; a winged goddess in a dream cloud; boxes rolling off a press.

    NIKE

    ANIMATIONDream cloud puffs; printing press clacks.

  6. 3.06MED8.7s

    Davidson didn't stay a 35-dollar footnote. In 1983, Knight gave her a gold swoosh ring with a diamond, and Nike shares.

    A small gift box opens to a gold ring; an envelope of stock certificates.

    ANIMATIONBox opens with a sparkle.

  7. 3.07MED9.8s

    In 1972, the first Nike-branded shoes showed up at the US Olympic trials in Eugene, including a hand-made racer runners called the Moon Shoe.

    Runners at the line in Eugene; a close-up of a shoe with a waffle print in the dirt.

    EUGENE · 1972

    ANIMATIONStarter's pistol; footprints left in the cinder.

  8. 3.08MED8.3s

    Money was so tight that American banks kept refusing credit. A Japanese trading company, Nissho Iwai, kept the business afloat.

    A bank door slamming; a Japanese banker sliding a cheque under it.

    ANIMATIONDoor slams; cheque slides.

  9. 3.09MED5.3s

    The Onitsuka split went to court. In 1974, Blue Ribbon Sports won.

    A gavel falls between two lawyers.

    1974 · WON

    ANIMATIONGavel bang.

Act 4: Air, and a Brand Without Factories

1:09 · 7 shots · 168 words
  1. 4.01MED10.6s

    Nike's first star was Steve Prefontaine, a fearless front-runner from Oregon. In 1975 he died in a car crash, aged 24. Nike's headquarters still honours him.

    A runner leading a pack; then a quiet memorial plaque.

    STEVE PREFONTAINE · 1951-1975

    ANIMATIONCrowd noise fades to silence.

  2. 4.02MED9.4s

    Then an aerospace engineer, Frank Rudy, pitched an odd idea that other companies had turned down: pockets of pressurised air inside the sole.

    An engineer with a blueprint of a sole with an air bubble.

    FRANK RUDY

    ANIMATIONBlueprint unrolls; bubble glows.

  3. 4.03MED9.4s

    Nike said yes. In 1978 it launched its first air-cushioned shoe. Nike Air would become one of the most valuable names in footwear.

    A shoe with a glowing pocket; NIKE AIR stamps on it.

    NIKE AIR · 1978

    ANIMATIONAir pocket inflates with a hiss.

  4. 4.04MED7.5s

    In 1980 the company went public. The accountant with a trunk full of shoes was suddenly very rich.

    Stock ticker; Knight looking stunned at a number.

    IPO · 1980

    ANIMATIONTicker scrolls; Knight's jaw drops.

  5. 4.05MED10.6s

    In 1987, designer Tinker Hatfield, who had trained as an architect, cut a window in the sole so you could see the air. The Air Max.

    A designer at a drafting board; a sole with a cut-out window.

    AIR MAX · 1987

    ANIMATIONCraft knife cuts a window; light shines through.

  6. 4.06MED10.2s

    Here's the real trick. Nike designs shoes, then pays contract factories, mostly in Asia, to make them. Today about half its shoes come from Vietnam.

    Map: design arrows from Oregon to factories in Asia; Vietnam highlighted.

    ~50% FROM VIETNAM

    ANIMATIONArrows fly across the Pacific.

  7. 4.07CU10.9s

    It spends its energy on what happens in your head when you see the swoosh. Anyone can copy a shoe. It's much harder to copy a feeling.

    A kid looking at a shoe in a shop window; a thought bubble of himself winning a race.

    ANIMATIONThought bubble swells; crowd cheer inside it.

Act 5: Jordan and Just Do It

1:18 · 8 shots · 190 words
  1. 5.01MED6.8s

    By 1984, Nike had a problem. Reebok had caught the aerobics craze and was racing ahead.

    Bar chart: a Reebok bar shooting past a Nike bar.

    ANIMATIONRival bar shoots up; Nike's stalls.

  2. 5.02MED8.3s

    So Nike bet most of its basketball budget on one rookie: Michael Jordan. The push came from consultant Sonny Vaccaro.

    Poker chips all pushed onto a single card with a basketball on it.

    ALL IN

    ANIMATIONChips slide; the table goes quiet.

  3. 5.03MED7.9s

    Jordan didn't want Nike. He wanted Adidas. His parents, especially his mother Deloris, got him to take the meeting.

    A young player arms crossed; his mother pointing him through a door.

    ANIMATIONDoor swings open.

  4. 5.04MED10.9s

    Nike offered about 500,000 dollars a year for five years, plus something unusual for the time: a cut of every shoe sold with his name on it.

    A contract with a royalty line circled.

    $500K/YEAR + ROYALTY

    ANIMATIONCircle draws; pen signs.

  5. 5.05CU15.8s

    You may have heard the NBA fined Jordan 5,000 dollars every game he wore the red-and-black shoe. The league did send a warning. Nike turned it into an ad about a banned shoe. A fine every game? No solid evidence.

    A 'BANNED' ad poster; a MYTH stamp lands half over it.

    MYTH CHECK

    ANIMATIONBANNED flashes; MYTH stamp thuds.

  6. 5.06MED9.8s

    Nike hoped for a few million dollars from Air Jordan in the first years. It sold more than 100 million in the first year.

    Revenue counter jumps; boxes fly off shelves.

    $100M+ IN YEAR ONE

    ANIMATIONCounter spins; boxes stream out.

  7. 5.07MED12.8s

    In 1988 the agency Wieden+Kennedy came up with three words: Just Do It. Dan Wieden said he adapted it from the last words of Gary Gilmore, a murderer executed in Utah.

    A typewriter clacking out the slogan; a shadowy prison wall behind.

    JUST DO IT · 1988

    ANIMATIONTypewriter keys clack; one letter at a time.

  8. 5.08MED5.3s

    By the early 1990s Nike had passed Reebok again and kept going.

    Bar chart: Nike's bar overtakes and keeps climbing.

    ANIMATIONNike bar shoots past.

Act 6: The Sweatshop Scandal

0:40 · 4 shots · 97 words
  1. 6.01MED10.2s

    Then the same machine that made Nike cool turned the world against it. Reporters found low wages, punishing hours and, in some supplier factories, children.

    A dim factory with rows of workers stitching.

    ANIMATIONSewing machines hum; a single bulb swings.

  2. 6.02MED9.1s

    In 1996, a magazine printed a photo of a boy in Pakistan stitching footballs with the swoosh. Campus protests followed across America.

    A magazine cover; then students with placards.

    1996

    ANIMATIONChants; placards bob.

  3. 6.03MED12.1s

    In 1998, Knight admitted the Nike name had become linked with slave wages, forced overtime and abuse. Nike raised minimum ages, allowed independent audits and later published its supplier list.

    Knight at a podium; a list of factories unrolls.

    1998

    ANIMATIONMicrophone feedback; the list unrolls.

  4. 6.04CU8.3s

    Critics said it wasn't enough. Supporters said Nike changed faster than most of the industry. That argument still goes on.

    Scales tipping back and forth.

    ANIMATIONScales wobble, never settle.

Act 7: Fast Forward

0:48 · 5 shots · 117 words
  1. 7.01MED11.7s

    From here the years fly. 1996: Nike signs a young golfer, Tiger Woods. 2003: it buys bankrupt Converse for about 305 million dollars, and signs an 18-year-old LeBron James.

    A timeline with icons popping on: golf ball, Converse star, a teenager in a jersey.

    1996 · 2003

    ANIMATIONTimeline scrolls; icons pop.

  2. 7.02MED8.3s

    2015: LeBron gets a lifetime deal, reportedly worth over a billion dollars. 2016: Knight's memoir, Shoe Dog, becomes a bestseller.

    A contract with LIFETIME stamped on it; a book on a shelf.

    LIFETIME DEAL

    ANIMATIONStamp thuds; book slides in.

  3. 7.03MED7.9s

    2017: Vaporfly shoes help runners break records so often that track officials later write new rules about shoe technology.

    Runners with springs in their shoes; a rulebook slamming shut.

    ANIMATIONBoing; rulebook slams.

  4. 7.04MED9.8s

    2018: an anniversary Just Do It ad with Colin Kaepernick. Some customers burned their shoes. Others bought more, and the ad won major awards.

    Split: someone burning shoes; a queue at a shop.

    2018

    ANIMATIONFlames on the left; till rings on the right.

  5. 7.05MED10.2s

    2019: Eliud Kipchoge, in Nike prototypes, runs a marathon distance in under two hours, in a special event that didn't count as an official record.

    A lone runner crossing a line; a clock showing 1:59.

    1:59:40

    ANIMATIONClock stops; crowd erupts.

Act 8: The Stumble and the Comeback

1:25 · 8 shots · 210 words
  1. 8.01MED12.4s

    In 2020, former eBay boss John Donahoe took over. His bet: sell directly through Nike's own apps and stores, and drop many of the shops that had sold Nike for decades.

    A phone app growing huge; shop doors closing one by one.

    DIRECT TO CONSUMER

    ANIMATIONDoors slam in sequence.

  2. 8.02MED9.4s

    For a while it worked. Then shoppers found other brands on the shelves Nike had left, and Nike leaned on re-releasing old favourites.

    Shop shelves filling with rival shoes; Nike reissuing the same box again and again.

    ANIMATIONSame box stamps out over and over.

  3. 8.03CU8.7s

    Remember the waffle iron? The company that once ruined kitchen appliances to invent something new was mostly selling its greatest hits.

    The waffle iron, cold and dusty on a shelf.

    ANIMATIONDust settles; a cobweb shimmers.

  4. 8.04MED10.6s

    Newer running brands like On and Hoka won over runners Nike used to own, and Nike's share price fell by more than half from its peak.

    A stock line sliding down; two new running shoes jogging past.

    -50%+

    ANIMATIONLine slides; runners overtake.

  5. 8.05MED9.4s

    In October 2024, Nike brought back Elliott Hill as CEO. He'd joined as an intern in 1988 and spent over 30 years there.

    An older man walking back through the campus gates; a 1988 intern badge.

    ELLIOTT HILL · 2024

    ANIMATIONGate swings open; footsteps.

  6. 8.06MED9.8s

    His plan: focus on athletes again, win back runners, footballers and basketball players, and make peace with the shops Nike had walked away from.

    Hill shaking hands with a small running-shop owner.

    ANIMATIONHandshake; shop bell.

  7. 8.07MED12.4s

    The numbers are still mixed. Revenue has been roughly flat at around 46 billion dollars, with sales in China and Converse falling hard, while running, football and basketball are growing again.

    Bar chart with some red bars falling and green bars rising.

    ~$46B · MIXED

    ANIMATIONRed bars dip; green bars climb.

  8. 8.08CU12.4s

    And remember Onitsuka? It became part of ASICS, which has spent recent years winning back serious runners. The company that gave Knight his first shoes is now one of his rivals.

    Two shoe brands side by side at a starting line.

    ANIMATIONStarter's pistol; both burst off.

Ending: A Feeling You Can Wear

0:30 · 4 shots · 62 words
  1. 9.01MED9.1s

    Almost every brand that sells you a lifestyle instead of a list of features owes something to a shoe company in Oregon.

    A wall of ads from other brands, all with athletes and slogans.

    ANIMATIONBillboards light up one by one.

  2. 9.02CU10.9s

    It started with a coach who hated heavy shoes, a runner with a car trunk full of them, and a waffle iron that never made waffles again.

    The trunk, the coach and the waffle iron together.

    ANIMATIONWaffle iron sizzles one last time.

  3. 9.03CU5.7s

    The question now is whether Nike can make you feel that way again.

    A kid lacing a shoe at a starting line.

    ANIMATIONLaces pull tight; a deep breath.

  4. 9.04TITLE4.0s

    (no narration)

    End card.

    HOW A WAFFLE IRON BUILT NIKE

    ANIMATIONSwoosh sound; fade.

Fact log

Fixes against the transcript

  • Bowerman spelled correctly (transcript: 'Bowererman'). Coached the 1972 US Olympic track team.
  • Knight's Stanford paper 1962; trip to Japan 1962 aged 24; Onitsuka in Kobe (transcript: 'Coobe').
  • BRS founded 1964 with $500 each; first-year sales about 1,300 pairs / ~$8,000.
  • Waffle iron 1971; Carolyn Davidson logo 1971, $35 at $2/hour; ring and shares in 1983.
  • Nissho Iwai (transcript: 'Nishouai') financed Nike when banks refused.
  • Converse bought 2003 for about $305 million (transcript said $35 million; corrected).
  • Jordan contract 1984: ~$500k/year for 5 years plus royalties; 'banned' fine-every-game story labelled as myth.
  • Just Do It (1988, Wieden+Kennedy; transcript 'Widen and Kennedy'); Gilmore origin per Dan Wieden.
  • Kipchoge (transcript 'Kipchigible') INEOS 1:59 Challenge 2019, 1:59:40, not an official record.
  • Elliott Hill CEO from 14 Oct 2024. CHECK before release: FY2026 revenue (~$46.4B per transcript), China/Converse declines; script keeps it to 'roughly flat at around 46 billion' and trends only.
  • About half of Nike footwear made in Vietnam per Nike's FY reports (~50%).

Removed from the transcript

  • 'Like and subscribe' outro removed.
  • Quarter-by-quarter FY2027 figures and the 'Pace' restructuring detail dropped (too fresh to verify).
  • World Cup 2026 marketing line dropped.
